title: Pressure after exertion
stem: A 58-year-old has 35 minutes of ongoing central chest pressure and sweating. BP is 128/78, pulse 92, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. No ECG has been recorded.

questions.prompt: Which investigation should be obtained immediately?

options.text: A 12-lead ECG
options.why: Ongoing ischemic symptoms warrant prompt ECG assessment; a normal oxygen saturation does not exclude ACS.

options.text: An outpatient exercise test
options.why: An outpatient stress test is not the initial assessment of ongoing acute symptoms.

options.text: A D-dimer before any cardiac testing
options.why: D-dimer is chosen through a PE probability pathway; it does not replace the initial ECG in this scenario.

questions.prompt: The first ECG is nondiagnostic, but pain continues. What follows?

options.text: Repeat ECG assessment and a validated serial troponin pathway
options.why: A single nondiagnostic tracing does not exclude ACS. Symptoms and serial testing guide the next steps.

options.text: Exclude ACS because the first ECG is normal
options.why: A single ECG cannot exclude ACS.

options.text: Exclude ACS after one negative early troponin regardless of timing
options.why: Rule-out depends on the assay, symptom timing and validated pathway, not an arbitrary single result.

title: A fast rhythm with poor perfusion
stem: A 67-year-old has a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 190/min, BP 72/40, chest pain and confusion. A pulse is present.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes this an unstable presentation?

options.text: Hypotension and altered mental status
options.why: Poor perfusion, rather than rate alone, establishes the urgency in this scenario.

options.text: The rate alone, regardless of perfusion
options.why: Rate contributes to assessment but must be interpreted with perfusion and symptoms.

options.text: A previous history of palpitations
options.why: Past episodes do not establish the stability of the current event.

questions.prompt: Which immediate approach fits this regular unstable tachycardia with a pulse?

options.text: Urgent synchronized cardioversion with the resuscitation team
options.why: A regular unstable tachycardia with a pulse calls for synchronized cardioversion; do not delay urgent care for a perfect diagnostic tracing.

options.text: Obtain an elective ambulatory monitor first
options.why: Ambulatory monitoring cannot address current hemodynamic instability.

options.text: Give verapamil for an undifferentiated wide-complex rhythm
options.why: Verapamil may cause severe deterioration in ventricular tachycardia.

title: Confusion during insulin treatment
stem: A 42-year-old using insulin becomes sweaty and confused after missing a meal. They are breathing normally with a pulse. A bedside glucose has not yet been checked.

questions.prompt: Which bedside measurement is immediately useful?

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.why: Hypoglycemia is a rapidly testable, reversible cause of altered mental status.

options.text: Head CT before checking glucose
options.why: Imaging may be needed, but a rapid bedside glucose identifies a treatable mimic without delaying the assessment.

options.text: A detailed neurological examination before any bedside glucose
options.why: Neurological assessment is important, but it should not postpone a rapid glucose check in this scenario.

questions.prompt: Glucose is 32 mg/dL and the patient cannot swallow safely. What is the safest principle?

options.text: Treat hypoglycemia promptly using a route that does not require swallowing
options.why: Severe hypoglycemia requires prompt correction; an unsafe swallow makes oral treatment inappropriate. Use the local emergency protocol.

options.text: Give a drink despite the unsafe swallow
options.why: Oral intake risks aspiration when swallowing is unsafe.

options.text: Wait for a fasting laboratory sample before treatment
options.why: Treatment of symptomatic severe hypoglycemia should not be delayed for a fasting sample.

title: Slow breathing after an opioid
stem: A 29-year-old is found difficult to rouse after taking an opioid. Respiratory rate is 5/min, pupils are small, and a pulse is present.

questions.prompt: What needs immediate support?

options.text: Airway and ventilation, with naloxone as appropriate
options.why: Inadequate breathing is the immediate threat. Support ventilation while addressing suspected opioid effects.

options.text: Observation alone because a pulse is present
options.why: A pulse does not make a respiratory rate of 5/min safe.

options.text: Activated charcoal before airway assessment
options.why: Airway and ventilation take priority, and aspiration risk must be considered.

questions.prompt: Breathing improves after naloxone. What remains necessary?

options.text: Continued reassessment for recurrent respiratory depression
options.why: The opioid effect can outlast reversal. Monitoring and reassessment remain important.

options.text: Immediate discharge solely because the patient awakens
options.why: An initial response does not establish a safe disposition.

options.text: Stop monitoring because the pupils have changed
options.why: Pupil size cannot replace respiratory and clinical reassessment.

title: Collapse with a warning symptom
stem: A 70-year-old briefly loses consciousness while walking. They now report chest pressure and palpitations. BP is 94/60. They are awake but pale.

questions.prompt: What should guide the initial assessment?

options.text: Evaluate for a cardiac or other dangerous cause with ECG and perfusion assessment
options.why: Chest symptoms, palpitations and low blood pressure make a reflex faint an unsafe assumption.

options.text: Diagnose a benign faint solely because consciousness returned
options.why: Recovery of consciousness does not identify the cause.

options.text: Arrange routine follow-up before checking an ECG
options.why: The warning features warrant immediate assessment.

questions.prompt: Which finding would further increase concern?

options.text: A high-grade conduction abnormality on ECG
options.why: A significant conduction abnormality can explain syncope and changes the urgency of care.

options.text: A normal temperature alone
options.why: Normal temperature does not resolve the cardiac concern.

options.text: A brief sensation of warmth before the event
options.why: Warmth can accompany reflex syncope, but it does not resolve the cardiac warning features in this case.

title: Ketosis with low potassium
stem: An adult with diabetes has vomiting, dehydration, glucose 420 mg/dL, ketonemia and metabolic acidosis. Potassium is 2.8 mmol/L.

questions.prompt: What treatment hazard needs attention before insulin?

options.text: The already low potassium
options.why: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can worsen hypokalemia. Follow the potassium replacement and monitoring pathway before starting insulin.

options.text: Start insulin immediately and replace potassium later
options.why: Insulin can further lower an already dangerous potassium level; replacement and monitoring must guide the initial sequence.

options.text: Assume the low serum potassium is harmless because acidosis is present
options.why: Low measured potassium in ketoacidosis is a serious treatment hazard, not reassurance about potassium stores.

questions.prompt: What monitoring principle is appropriate?

options.text: Serial electrolytes, glucose and clinical reassessment
options.why: Treatment changes glucose, volume and potassium; repeated measurements guide safe adjustment.

options.text: Use the initial potassium for the entire treatment period
options.why: Potassium can change substantially during treatment.

options.text: Assess recovery only by whether vomiting stops
options.why: Symptom improvement does not establish correction of the metabolic disturbance.

title: Back pain with new bladder symptoms
stem: A 46-year-old has severe low back pain, new urinary retention, saddle numbness and bilateral leg weakness.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis needs urgent exclusion?

options.text: Cauda equina compression
options.why: New bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory change and bilateral weakness are a concerning combination.

options.text: Uncomplicated muscular strain without further assessment
options.why: The neurological and bladder findings are not explained safely by a simple strain label.

options.text: Simple cystitis as the sole explanation
options.why: Cystitis does not explain the saddle sensory change and bilateral weakness.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate next direction?

options.text: Urgent neurological assessment and spinal imaging/specialist pathway
options.why: This pattern needs urgent assessment for compression and prompt escalation through the local pathway.

options.text: Routine exercise advice with no urgent workup
options.why: Red-flag neurological symptoms require urgent evaluation.

options.text: Delay review until a routine physiotherapy appointment
options.why: A routine appointment is not sufficient for suspected acute compression.

title: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain
stem: A 16-year-old develops abrupt severe unilateral scrotal pain with nausea. The affected testis is high-riding and very tender.

questions.prompt: Which time-sensitive diagnosis is most concerning?

options.text: Testicular torsion
options.why: Abrupt pain and an abnormal testicular lie raise concern for torsion.

options.text: Epididymitis as the leading explanation
options.why: Infection can cause scrotal pain, but the sudden onset and high-riding testis make torsion the immediate concern.

options.text: Torsion of a testicular appendage as the leading explanation
options.why: Appendage torsion can cause acute pain, but does not safely account for the high-risk testicular position and presentation here.

questions.prompt: Which principle should guide the next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical assessment; imaging must not delay care when suspicion is high
options.why: Testicular viability is time-sensitive. Follow the urgent local surgical pathway.

options.text: Delay until the next routine clinic appointment
options.why: Routine follow-up risks losing time in torsion.

options.text: Wait for pain to resolve before seeking an opinion
options.why: Temporary symptom changes do not safely exclude torsion.

title: Bleeding with circulatory compromise
stem: A 64-year-old vomits blood and has black stools. BP is 78/44, pulse 126, and the patient is cool and clammy.

questions.prompt: What is the first priority?

options.text: Resuscitation and urgent escalation for hemorrhage
options.why: The patient shows circulatory compromise. Stabilization proceeds alongside source assessment.

options.text: Complete a formal bleeding risk score before obtaining vascular access
options.why: Risk tools help later decisions but must not delay resuscitation for overt circulatory compromise.

options.text: Prioritize endoscopy preparation before supporting circulation
options.why: Source control is important, but circulatory support and urgent escalation must proceed immediately.

questions.prompt: After initial treatment, what guides further care?

options.text: Repeated perfusion assessment and coordinated bleeding control
options.why: An initial response can be temporary. Reassess while arranging definitive assessment and control.

options.text: One improved blood pressure ends the assessment
options.why: One reading does not establish sustained stability or bleeding control.

options.text: Stool color alone proves bleeding has stopped
options.why: Stool appearance is not a sufficient measure of current circulation or bleeding.

title: New unilateral weakness
stem: A 73-year-old develops right arm weakness and difficulty speaking. Last known well was 40 minutes ago. A pulse is present and the airway is currently patent.

questions.prompt: Which early information and test are essential?

options.text: Document last known well and check bedside glucose
options.why: Time of onset and glucose are key early parts of the stroke assessment.

options.text: Use the time the patient was found as the onset time
options.why: Time found is not necessarily last known well; document the actual timing history.

options.text: Complete medication reconciliation before measuring glucose
options.why: Medication history matters, but should not delay a rapid bedside glucose or time-sensitive stroke assessment.

questions.prompt: What should happen next?

options.text: Activate the stroke pathway with urgent brain imaging
options.why: Urgent imaging and specialist assessment guide treatment eligibility and distinguish hemorrhage from ischemia.

options.text: Start anticoagulation before brain imaging
options.why: Treatment must account for possible hemorrhage and follow the stroke pathway.

options.text: Book routine imaging for the following week
options.why: A routine timeline is inappropriate for an acute focal deficit.

title: Wheeze after a food exposure
stem: Minutes after eating peanuts, a 22-year-old develops widespread hives, wheeze and dizziness. BP is 82/48.

questions.prompt: Which pattern does this suggest?

options.text: Anaphylaxis with respiratory and circulatory involvement
options.why: Rapid symptoms involving skin, breathing and circulation after exposure strongly support anaphylaxis.

options.text: An isolated mild skin reaction
options.why: Wheeze and hypotension show involvement beyond the skin.

options.text: Anxiety alone because the onset was sudden
options.why: Anxiety does not explain this combination of objective findings.

questions.prompt: Which treatment should not be delayed?

options.text: Intramuscular epinephrine with emergency support
options.why: Epinephrine is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; airway, breathing and circulation also require support.

options.text: Antihistamine alone as definitive treatment
options.why: Antihistamines do not treat the life-threatening airway or circulatory components.

options.text: Wait for a blood test to confirm the allergy
options.why: Anaphylaxis is assessed clinically and urgent treatment must not await laboratory confirmation.

title: Abrupt deterioration during positive-pressure ventilation
stem: A ventilated patient suddenly becomes hypoxic and hypotensive. Breath sounds are absent on one side, and chest movement is asymmetric.

questions.prompt: Which immediate threat must be considered?

options.text: Tension pneumothorax
options.why: Sudden respiratory and circulatory deterioration with unilateral findings raises concern for tension physiology.

options.text: An isolated mucus plug without another complication
options.why: A mucus plug is a competing cause of sudden hypoxia; the associated hypotension and unilateral findings make tension pneumothorax an immediate threat to assess.

options.text: Pulmonary edema as the sole explanation
options.why: Pulmonary edema does not as readily explain abruptly absent unilateral breath sounds and asymmetric chest movement.

questions.prompt: If clinical assessment strongly supports tension pneumothorax, what principle applies?

options.text: Urgent decompression by the treating team without waiting for imaging
options.why: In an unstable patient with a compelling clinical picture, imaging must not delay treatment.

options.text: Transfer for routine CT before any intervention
options.why: Transport and imaging can dangerously delay care in this unstable scenario.

options.text: Observe until the next ward round
options.why: The deterioration requires immediate response.
